description: Knechtle presents his return to Christianity as the result of accumulated evidence and rejecting hedonism as bankrupt, thereby asserting that faith had rational warrant.
critique: Strongest feature: Knechtle’s first-person sequence—rejecting hedonism’s “bankruptcy,” then returning after seeing “all this evidence”—intelligibly challenges Dillahunty’s claim that Christianity lacks warrant. Principal limitation: Neither the evidence nor hedonism’s alleged inadequacy is specified, and abandoning hedonism does not establish Christianity; consequently, it never meets Dillahunty’s reality-consistency test or demand for verifiable support. Live burden: Knechtle must identify the considerations, explain how they connect rejection of hedonism to Christian belief, and demonstrate why they remain assessable beyond the private force of his conversion experience. Locked score: 64 recognizes clear autobiographical structure, measured personal framing, reply contact, and motion relevance, while reserving substantial credit because the decisive evidence is unauditable here, the comparative inference is incomplete, and the opponent’s evidential standard remains unanswered.
